deep.reconstruction:
Context: elementary lecture notes on the arithmetic of the integers. The previous page treated commutativity and associativity of products and the transitivity of divisibility. The next page gives the Euclidean algorithm. This page supplies the basic definitions between them.

(1) Closure of multiples. If c divides m-type quantities, i.e. given multiples cm and cn of c, then cm ± cn = c(m ± n). So the sum and difference of multiples of a number are again multiples of it. Multiples may be negative, and 0 = c·0 is a multiple of every number.

(2) Synonyms. 'a is a multiple of b' is equivalent to each of the following: 'b is a factor (divisor) of a'; 'a is divisible by b'; 'a goes out evenly by b'; 'b goes into a'. In modern notation: b | a  <=>  there is an integer k with a = kb.

(3) Classification of single numbers. Every number n is a multiple of itself and of 1. Some numbers are multiples only of themselves and 1; these are the primes (numeri primi). The rest are composite (numeri compositi). Examples: 7 is prime, 12 is composite.

(4) Classification of pairs. A second classification concerns systems of numbers rather than a single number. For example, 12 and 15 have the common divisor 3, while 12 and 35 have no common divisor other than 1. Pairs of the latter kind are 'relatively prime' (gcd = 1). Of the former one says 'they have a common divisor or common divisors'.

(5) Problem posed: given two numbers, find their common divisor(s). This motivates the gcd and the Euclidean algorithm on the next page. That algorithm rests on fact (1): every common divisor of a and b also divides c = a − mb, and conversely.
errors: Not an error so much as a gap: under the stated definition (a number that is a multiple only of itself and of 1), the number 1 would qualify as prime. The note does not explicitly exclude 1, nor 0 and negative numbers, from the prime/composite classification.
Common divisors ±1 are tacitly ignored when 12 and 35 are said to have no common divisor. This is standard informal usage.

results.what: Sums and differences of multiples of c are multiples of c: cm ± cn = c(m ± n); 0 is a multiple of every number
results.modern_name: Multiples of c form an ideal cZ (closure under subtraction)

results.what: Definition of divisor/multiple and of prime versus composite numbers, with examples 7 and 12
Relatively prime numbers versus numbers with a common divisor (12, 15 vs 12, 35); problem of finding common divisors

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard introductory definitions from elementary number theory, apparently lecture notes. They follow Euclid and Dirichlet-style presentation and contain nothing novel.
